newsitem.title: LATVIA: Latvian premier-designate pledges faster reform.
newsitem.headline: Latvian premier-designate pledges faster reform.

text.p: The prime minister-designate of Latvia pledged on Friday to speed up the reforms launched after the country quit the former Soviet Union six years ago.
Guntar Krasts has been chosen to replace Andris Shkele, forced to resign after quarrels with the seven parties that formed his unwieldy cabinet.
Krasts told state-owned Radio Latvia in an interview that the Baltic republic needed a better economic performance.
"We have to achieve better (economic) results in the second part of 1997 and in 1998 and therefore we have to increase the pace of reform," Krasts said.
Shkele, a tough businessman with no party affiliation, was credited with giving fresh impetus to reforms despite a squabbling seven-party coalition.
Krasts, 39, from the nationalist group For Fatherland and Freedom, was economy minister in Shkele's 18-month government and has the reputation of a reformist.
But he is untested and commentators say he may have a tough job keeping reforms going given the rainbow nature of his coalition.
The new government is likely to be largely unchanged from Shkele's coalition, a mix of right-wingers and left-of-centre parties that had 70 seats in the 100-seat parliament.
Shkele managed to pass a balanced budget for 1997 and get Latvia's finances in order.
A deficit-free budget is now in doubt due to an income tax shortfall but Krasts insisted a balanced budget was his goal.
"We will aim to achieve a balanced budget in 1997, and even if we fail, it is a must for 1998, which we will implement."
